title: Talk on jobs in fashion design
transcript:
Speaker 0: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
Speaker 1: Hi, Chantal. What did you think of the talk then?
Speaker 2: Hi, Hugo. I thought it was good once I'd moved seats.
Speaker 1: Oh, were the people beside you chatting or something?
Speaker 2: It wasn't that. I went early so that I'd get a seat and not have to stand. But then this guy sat right in front of me, and he was so tall.
Speaker 1: It's hard to see through people's heads, isn't it?
Speaker 2: Impossible. Anyway, to answer your question, I thought it was really interesting, especially what the speaker said about the job market.
Speaker 1: Me too. I mean, we know we're going into a really competitive field, so it's obvious that we may struggle to get work.
Speaker 2: That's right. And we know we can't all have that dream job.
Speaker 1: Yeah. But it looks like there's a whole range of areas of work that we hadn't even thought of, like fashion journalism, for instance.
Speaker 2: Yeah. I wasn't expecting so many career options.
Speaker 1: Overall, she had quite a strong message, didn't she?
Speaker 2: She did. She kept saying things like, I know you all think this, but and then she'd tell us how it really is.
Speaker 1: Perhaps she thinks students are a bit narrow minded about the industry.
Speaker 2: It was a bit harsh, though. We know it's a tough industry.
Speaker 1: Yeah. And we're only first years after all. We've got a lot to learn.
Speaker 2: Exactly. Do you think our secondary school education should have been more career focused?
Speaker 1: Well, we had numerous talks on careers, which was good, but none of them were very inspiring. They could have asked more people like today's speaker to talk to us.
Speaker 2: I agree. We were told about lots of different careers, just when we needed to be, but not by the experts who really know stuff.
Speaker 1: So did today's talk influence your thoughts on what career you'd like to take up in the future?
Speaker 2: Well, I promised myself that I'd go through this course and keep an open mind till the end.
Speaker 1: But I think it's better to pick an area of the industry now and then aim to get better and better at it.
Speaker 2: Well, I think we'll just have to differ on that issue.
Speaker 1: One thing's for certain, though. From what she said, we'll be unpaid assistance in industry for quite a long time. I'm prepared for that. Aren't you?
Speaker 2: Actually, I'm not going to accept that view.
Speaker 1: Really? But she knows it's the case, and everyone else says the same.
Speaker 2: That doesn't mean it has to be true for me.
Speaker 1: Okay. Well, I hope you're right.
Speaker 0: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
Speaker 2: I thought the speaker's account of her first job was fascinating.
Speaker 1: Yeah. She admitted she was lucky to get work being a personal dresser for a musician. She didn't even apply for the job, and there she was getting paid to choose all his clothes.
Speaker 2: It must have felt amazing. Though she said all she was looking for back then was experience, not financial reward.
Speaker 1: And then he was so mean telling her she was more interested in her own appearance than his.
Speaker 2: But she did realize he was right about that, which really made me think. I'm always considering my own clothes, but now I can see you should be focusing on your client.
Speaker 1: She obviously regretted losing the job.
Speaker 2: Well, as she said, she should have hidden her negative feelings about him, but she didn't.
Speaker 1: It was really brave the way she picked herself up and took that job in retail. Fancy working in a shop after that?
Speaker 2: Yeah. Well, she recommended we all do it at some point. I guess, as a designer, you'd get to find out some useful information, like how big or small the average shopper is.
Speaker 1: I think that's an issue for manufacturers, not designers. However, it would be useful to know if there's a gap in the market, you know, an item that no one's stocking, but that consumers are looking for.
Speaker 2: Yeah. People don't give up searching. They also take things back to the store if they aren't right.
Speaker 1: Yeah. Imagine you worked in an expensive shop, and you found out the garments sold there were being returned because they fell apart in the wash.
Speaker 2: Yeah. It would be good to know that kind of thing.
Speaker 1: Yeah.
Speaker 0: That is the end of part three. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part three. Part four. You will hear a zoology student giving a presentation on the process of moving wild elephants to a new reserve known as translocation. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
